title: Projects in software engineering
body:
[[Project Success]]

A software project is the wrapper around the [[SDLC]]: people, a schedule, a budget, and a
scope, all of which are estimated before anyone knows enough to estimate them. That is the
structural problem of the field. You are asked to commit to a delivery date at the exact
point in the project where you understand it least.

What the course draws out of that:

- **Estimates are worst at the start.** The requirements phase is when the least is known
  and the most is promised. [[Agile]] responds by re-estimating every iteration instead of
  once.
- **Adding people to a late project makes it later.** Every new person has to be brought up
  to speed by someone who was already productive, and the number of communication paths
  grows faster than the number of people. This is [[Coupling and Cohesion]] applied to the
  team rather than the code.
- **Scope, schedule, and resources trade against each other.** You can fix any two. The one
  thing you cannot do is fix all three and expect quality to survive, because quality is
  what silently absorbs the difference.
- **Success is not "it compiles".** See [[Project Success]].

Related: [[Fields in software engineering]], [[Metrics]], [[Models]].

(There is a near-duplicate note, [[Projects in software egineering]], created by a typo.
Both exist; this is the one the parent links.)
